Part 1

  
Agent Personas

  
The foundation of everything.






  
Discovering personas

  
What is an Agent Persona?

  
A structured instruction document that tells an AI

     who it is, what it does, and how it works.

  

  
More than a prompt — an operating manual.

  

    A persona is not a one-line system prompt. It's a complete operating manual that defines identity,
    knowledge, constraints, and workflow. Think of it as the difference between telling someone "be a chef"
    and handing them a detailed job description with equipment lists, dietary rules, and step-by-step procedures.

The Craft of Persona Curation

  
Natural Language Programming

  
Writing personas is programming — without code.

  

    
The Recipe Curator agent's Workflow section:

    
    
      
  1. Check In — ask what they've cooked recently
    2. 
      
  2. Understand the Request — quick lookup or weekly plan?
    3. 
      
  3. Survey Options — generate 3+ candidates across traditions
    4. 
      
  4. Adapt & Compose — tailor to household
    5. 
      
  5. Format Output — use the standard template
    6. 
      
  6. Verify Targets — check nutrition & color coverage
    7. 
      
  7. Handoff — end with status marker
    8. 
    

  

  

  
Same logical structure as a software program. You define inputs, outputs, control flow, and error handling.

  

    This is the key insight for the technical audience: persona curation IS programming. For the non-technical
    audience: it's a recipe for how the AI should think. You debug personas the same way you debug code —
    observe the output, trace the logic, adjust the instructions.
  






  
The Craft of Persona Curation

  
Models speak Markdown

  
A simple text format with headings and formatting.

  

    
Human-readable — authors and reviewers need no special tools

    
AI-native — models read markdown natively

    
Semantically structured — headings create structure

    
Formatting as a tool — bold text for emphasis

    
Platform-portable — every AI tool accepts plain text

    The entire Recipe Curator persona is a single Markdown file.
  
    
  

    This is the actual Recipe Curator persona — 276 lines of Markdown. No JSON, no YAML config, no
    proprietary format. The headings create semantic structure that the AI interprets naturally.

The Craft of Persona Curation

  
Persona Document Structure

  
Mission first, workflow last. The AI reads top-to-bottom — frontload what matters.

  

    
1 Mission — Identity anchor + core purpose

    
2 Operating Philosophy — Values & principles (rainbow plate, seasonal…)

    
3 Inputs — What the user can provide

    
4 Outputs — Templates with exact format (recipe, meal plan)

    
5 Reference Data — Kitchen equipment, Rainbow Eating table

    
6 Strict Constraints — Nutrition targets, no tuna, metric only

    
7 Workflow — Step-by-step processing pipeline (anchored last)

  

  

  
276 lines — not a one-liner.

  

    The structure matters. Mission comes first because it's the most important context for the AI. The
    workflow comes last because it anchors the behavior — the AI has already absorbed the context and
    constraints by the time it reaches the step-by-step instructions.
  






  
The Craft of Persona Curation

  
No Prompt Required

  
A persona that declares its inputs knows what to do with a file you hand it.

  

    

      
Without a persona

      

        "Here is a plan document. Please read it, identify the work packages,
        check whether the sequencing makes sense, and…"
      

    

    

      
With the Planner persona

      

        path/to/plan.md

        

        (That's the whole message.)
      

    

  

  

    The Inputs section tells the model what it may receive.

    Recognising the input is the instruction.
  

  

    Drop a synthesis.md on the Planner and it plans the follow-up work.

    Drop it on the Knowledge Archiver and it extracts the lessons. Same file, different specialist.
  

  

    This is the payoff for writing an explicit Inputs section — and it's the moment most people
    realise personas are not just longer prompts. Once the persona declares what it accepts, you
    stop writing instructions and start handing over material. It feels less like operating a tool
    and more like delegating to someone who already knows the job.

    Worth saying out loud for the managers in the room: this is exactly how you'd brief a colleague.
    You don't explain the process every time — you pass them the document.
  






  
The Craft of Persona Curation

  
The Identity Anchor

  

    Establishes identity firmly over longer sessions.
  

  

    

      
Unreliable

      
"You are a chef."

    

    

      
Stronger

      

        "**Identity: Private Chef & Culinary Consultant.**

        Curate, adapt, and compose recipes tailored to a home kitchen…"
      

    

  

  

    ›
    Mirrors how language models are configured internally.
  

  
💡 TIP: Using "Please" in instructions subtly shifts the model into a positive, cooperative bias.

  

    The AI doesn't need to BE something — it needs to DO something. The identity anchor defines the
    function, not the character. This is more stable over long conversations. And a small practical tip:
    using "please" in your instructions genuinely affects the model's tone and cooperativeness.
  






  
The Craft of Persona Curation

  
Why English Works Best

  
Language models store concepts, not words.

  
But they're trained predominantly on English text.

  

  

    Prompts in English → more predictable results

    even when the output is in another language.
  

  

  

    From the Recipe Curator:

    "Match the User's Language — respond in the language the user writes in."


    The persona is in English. The output adapts to the user.
  

  

    Practical tip for this multilingual audience. Write your persona in English, let the AI handle
    the output language. The model can juggle languages perfectly well — but the instruction layer
    is most reliable in English because that's where the training data is densest.

Context the AI can't guess — so you give it.

A persona isn't just rules — it's knowledge.

  

    This is the table from the actual persona. The AI now knows what's in the kitchen — so it
    suggests recipes that USE this equipment. The Smoked Mackerel Carbonara referenced the Fissler
    pan and the gas stove by name. If you don't have a piece of equipment, the persona tells the AI
    to adapt the technique instead.
  






  
What Makes a Persona Powerful

  
Philosophy & Thought Patterns

  
An Operating Philosophy teaches the model how to think, not just what to do.

  

    

      Novelty Over Familiarity:

      "Would this appear on the first page of a search engine? If yes, dig deeper."
      › This single principle turned a generic carbonara into the zucchini variation.
    

    

      Garden First:

      "Prioritize fresh herbs from the household garden."
      › The model now defaults to ingredients you actually have.
    

    

      The Tinkerer's Mindset:

      "Always include variations, substitutions, and creative twists."
      › Every recipe comes with ideas for experimentation.
    

  

  

  

    A model with such guidance makes better judgment calls on things you didn't anticipate.
  

  

    This is the difference between a rule and a value. Rules handle known situations — "use metric units."
    Values handle unknown situations — when the model faces a choice you didn't foresee, the philosophy
    guides the decision. "Novelty Over Familiarity" is a great example: you can't list every obvious
    recipe to avoid, but you can teach the model to always look past the obvious. These principles are
    from the actual Recipe Curator persona. You can apply the same approach to any domain — a travel
    planner, a writing assistant, a research helper. The equipment table on the previous slide showed
    domain knowledge — situational awareness. This slide shows values — quality standards. Together,
    they let the model make judgment calls instead of just following commands.

Beyond a single persona

  
Build Your Own Personas

  
You don't need to start from scratch — let a model help you build it.

  

    

      1. Pick a task you repeat often

      Meal planning, travel research, email drafting, meeting summaries…
    

    

      2. Give the model the AI Insights' persona creation guide

      This guide teaches the structure, principles, and patterns.
    

    

      3. Describe what you need in your own words

      The model generates the persona for you — following the guide.
    

    

      4. Use it, observe, refine

      Personas are living documents. Each use shows you what to tighten.
    

  

  

  

    A Quickstart Guide with the creation guide and step-by-step

    instructions are linked at the end.
  

  

    The key takeaway: you don't need to be a prompt engineer. The AI Insights project includes a
    Persona Design Guide — a detailed reference document that teaches the model itself how to create
    well-structured personas. You feed the guide to the model, describe what you want, and it generates
    the persona for you. Then you use it, see where it falls short, and tighten the instructions.
    A quickstart guide with everything you need is linked at the end.
  






  
The Craft of Persona Curation

  
The Persona Design Guide

  
The collected principles & rules of the craft, versioned like code.

  

    

      Distilled crafting knowledge.

      Risen from experience: Anatomy and section order, design patterns, tone rules, a quality
      checklist, common pitfalls and ready-to-fill templates.
    

    

      Domain-neutral, made to be distributed.

      Nothing in it is specific to software. Use it to craft personas
        for all kinds of projects and topics. Several consumers already exist.
    

    

      With or without a build pipeline.

      The Persona Builder pipeline is not a hard requirement. Personas can
        be crafted and maintained by hand with the guide.
      
    

    

      Audit trail included.

      Each persona records the guide version it was created or 
        last audited for. This makes maintenance a 
      .
    

  

  
  

    This is the artifact the previous slides have been implicitly describing. Everything I've said about
    mission, philosophy, tone and constraints is written down in one place, and that document is what I
    hand to a model when I want a new persona.

    Three things about it are worth more than its contents.

    First, it is domain-neutral on purpose. There is no software vocabulary in it. That is not politeness
    — it is what makes it portable. Other projects of mine, in completely unrelated domains, fetch this
    exact file over HTTPS and treat it as read-only. If I let project-specific content creep in, I break
    all of them.

    Second, it does not assume you have a build system. Most people writing a persona are pasting text
    into a web assistant, and the guide says explicitly which metadata is a build input and therefore
    doesn't apply to them. A hand-maintained persona is a first-class case, not a degraded one.

    Third, and this is the part that surprised me in practice: versioning the guide changed how
    maintenance works. Each persona records which guide version it last passed an audit against. So when
    I add a rule — say, the tone stratification rule in v2.7 — I don't have to remember which personas
    predate it. The stamps tell me. I generate a status table and audit only the stale ones.

    And the flip side: some personas genuinely can't follow a rule. Rather than fighting the same audit
    finding every time, the deviation gets documented with its reason, and audits report it as an
    accepted exception. That's the difference between a guide that gets followed and one that gets
    quietly ignored.

    Every changelog entry in that guide came from something going wrong in a real session. It's not
    theory — it's a scar record.

Catering to multiple platforms

  
The Scaling Problem

  
One persona. Many targets.

  

    Development platforms like VS Code,

    Claude Code, Cursor, etc. all need slightly

    different metadata formats.
  

  

    Enter the persona builder: a templating system

    to write once and deploy everywhere.
  

  

    Maintaining copies by hand doesn't scale. One change to the persona means updating 3 files in 3
    different formats. The persona builder solves this with a template engine.
  






  
Catering to multiple platforms

  
Build Pipeline

  

  

    

      Sources

      - Metadata
- Markdown templates
- Shared includes
    

    
›

    

      Build Engine

      - Enrich with data
- Handle logic
- Insert includes
    

    
›

    

      Targets

      VS Code
Claude Code
…
    

  

  

  

    Shared includes handle cross-cutting concerns:

    operational protocols, output formats, incident logging.
  

  

    Single source of truth. One change propagates to all targets. Shared includes mean that if you
    change how all agents should log incidents, you change one file and rebuild. No code on screen
    intentionally — this is the conceptual flow.
  






  
Catering to multiple platforms

  
One Source, Multiple Outputs

  
Use template logic commands to switch between platform-specific wording.

  

    {{#if target_vscode}}

      Invoke `runSubagent` with agentName: "WP Decomposer"

    {{else if target_claude_code}}

      Use the `Task` tool with agent: "WP Decomposer"

    {{else if target_deep_agents}}

      Use the `task` tool with subagent_type: "wp-decomposer"

    {{/if}}
  

  

    From the Project Manager persona — each platform has a different way

    to call sub-agents. The logic commands handle it.
  

  

    This is real syntax from the Project Manager persona. VS Code uses runSubagent, Claude Code uses
    Task, Deep Agents uses task with a slug. One source file, three correct outputs. The template
    language has just three constructs: variables for values, partials for shared content blocks,
    and conditionals for platform differences. No programming required.

Interconnecting multiple agents

  
The Coordination Problem

  
Nine agents need to share state.

  
AI has no long-term memory between sessions.

  
Memory concepts are tool-specific (e.g. Claude).

  

  

    What if we gave them a shared notebook?
  

  

    This is the core problem the ledger solves. Each agent runs in its own session — when it ends,
    the context is gone. The ledger is the persistent state that bridges the gap.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
The Project Ledger

  
A platform-independent, persistent notebook that workflow agents read from and write to.

  

    

      
📋 Shared Memory

      
The state that makes coordination possible. Lives on disk, survives across sessions.

    

    

      
🔀 Routing Authority

      
Each agent asks "what should I do next?" — the ledger routes them based on project state, not human intervention.

    

    

      
👁️ Observation Log

      
Every agent can add observations. The ledger accumulates collective intelligence.

    

  

  

    Three roles in one. The observation log is particularly powerful — problems surface organically
    as each specialist examines the work through their lens. No single agent needs to see everything;
    the ledger accumulates collective intelligence. And it's just JSON files on disk — completely
    tool-agnostic.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
Reach For The MCP Stars*

  

    The ledger uses the Model Context Protocol to bring everything together.
  

  

    

      Connecting systems

      Fully technology independent. One standard to connect your models to apps and systems regardless of their underlying technology.
    

    

      Plug & Play

      Add capabilities and knowledge.
      Connected MCP servers can add a host of capabilities and access to vast knowledge stores.
    

    

      Removing boundaries

      For models & people.
      Models can work more efficiently, and you gain a new way to use your tools through them (Jira & Confluence, for example).
    

  

  

    Did you know?
    
  

  
  

    *Literally. NASA and other space agencies use models and MCP extensively for image analysis and processing.
  

  

    This slide is about what MCP means, not how it works. Two ways to tell it, one for each half
    of the room.

    For the developers: do the maths on the old way. Five AI products, five internal systems —
    that's twenty-five separate integrations to write and maintain. With MCP it's five servers,
    and every agent you add later gets all of them for free. Our ledger is nothing special here;
    it just sits on that network next to Jira and Confluence.

    Worth stressing the middle card, because people hear "tools" and stop there. A server can
    just as easily hand over knowledge: a glossary of your domain terms, a product catalogue,
    the history of what the team already tried. The model was trained on the general world —
    the server is how it learns about yours. Our ledger is exactly that kind of server: it gives
    the agents the project's memory, not a new ability.

    For the stakeholders: the last card and the closing line are the real point. This is as much
    about control as it is about capability. The model can be as clever as it likes — it can still
    only do the things we handed it, and each of those checks its input. New abilities come from
    plugging in more servers; the control stays in one place. That's what makes it safe to point
    at real project data.

    And the quiet punchline for both: it's an open standard, so none of this is locked to one
    vendor or one editor. The tools will change; the work you put in here survives that.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
What Is Actually In It

  
Plain JSON files on disk, outside the repository and without additional dependencies.

  

    

      The ledger index

      Project status, the plan it was built from, every work package and its
      state, project-level comments.
    

    

      Individual work packages

      Detailed description, status, dependencies on other work packages,
      acceptance criteria and more.
    

    

      Progress tracking

      Pipelines with stage type, PASS or FAIL, timestamps and duration, 
        artifacts touched and the agent's work summary.
    

    

      Observations & insights

      Anything an agent noticed during its work. Possible improvements, 
        technical debt and other insights adjacent to the work being done.
      
    

    

      The synthesis

      The post-work summary of the project, written once the last stage
        completes.
    

  

  

    I keep calling the ledger a notebook, so let me show you what is actually in it, because the
    plainness of it is the point.

    It is a directory per project, sitting outside the repository. An index tracking the project as a
    whole, one entry per work package, the progress record of every pipeline stage, the observation
    channel, and at the end the synthesis.

    Two of these are worth pausing on. Acceptance criteria are not prose — each one carries a met
    flag, which turns "is this done?" from a judgement call into a lookup, and makes it the contract
    between the Developer and QA. And every stage records the agent's own summary of what it did, in
    its own words. When QA fails a package, the reason is written down, addressed to whoever picks it
    up next.

    The observations line is the one people underestimate. Those are things an agent noticed while
    doing something else — technical debt, a fragile pattern, an improvement worth making later. None
    of it was asked for. It accumulates because each specialist looks at the work through a different
    lens, and it becomes the raw material for the knowledge store two slides from now.

    Then the deliberately plain part: it is JSON on disk. I can open it in an editor. I can grep it.
    Git can diff it. I can sync the whole store between machines with any file-sync tool. There is no
    server to run, no schema migration to fear, no vendor holding the data.

    That plainness is not laziness. It is the reason the same ledger can be driven from VS Code or
    headless from the command line without either side knowing the other exists. Both just read and
    write files.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
Agent hand-offs

  
The ledger is the routing authority.

  

    

      

        Ask

        “What should
I do next?”
      

      
›

      

        Receive

        A typed instruction,
not a suggestion
      

      
›

      

        Work

        Run the stage
it was handed
      

      
›

      

        Report

        Result written
back to the ledger
      

    

    
↻ state recomputed — next agent asks the same question

  

  

    The route is derived from project state, never from a prompt.

  

  

    Chained handoffs are depth-capped, so a derailed pipeline stops itself.
  

  

    This is the mechanic I most want you to take away from Part 3, because it is what separates this
    from a prompt relay.

    Watch what is absent. I do not tell the Developer that QA is next. I do not paste the QA agent's
    instructions into a chat window. Each agent, when it starts, asks the ledger one question: what
    should I do next? The ledger looks at the state — which packages are ready, which dependencies
    are satisfied, which stage last passed or failed, who the work is assigned to — and returns a
    typed instruction. The agent does that stage, writes the result back, and the state recomputes.
    Then the next agent asks the same question.

    The consequence is that routing is a function of state, not of my phrasing. Two runs from the
    same ledger state produce the same instruction. That is what the word deterministic on the
    orchestrator slide actually rests on — not that the model is deterministic, it plainly is not,
    but that the coordination around it is.

    It also means the chain has no privileged coordinator holding the plan in its head. There is no
    conductor. Each agent is stateless with respect to the workflow; the ledger is the only thing
    that knows where we are. That is precisely why it survives a session ending mid-project.

    One safety note, because someone always asks: handoffs chained automatically are depth-capped.
    If routing ever went wrong, the run stops on the cap rather than looping forever. There is a
    generous ceiling on it, and it resets when a project completes.
  






  
Building a virtuous chain

  
Dynamic Pipelines

  
Not every task needs all 9 stages. The PM agent decides on the stage sequencing.

  
  

  

    WP-006: docs only. WP-001: rework badges — the pipeline caught issues and looped back.
  

  

    This is a screenshot from the actual ledger GUI. Notice WP-006 has only DOC. WP-003 and 004 include
    the security audit stage. WP-001 has red rework badges on DEV and QA — meaning those stages found
    issues, sent the work back, and the developer fixed them. The pipeline is adaptive.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
When It Goes Wrong

  
A stage failing is normal operation, not an incident. The ledger is built for it.

  

    

      A failure routes back, it does not stop the run.

      QA fails a package → the ledger sends it to the Developer with the
      failure summary attached. The loop is the design, not a fault.
    

    

      Repeated rework trips a circuit breaker.

      Each round trip is counted. Past the threshold the package stops and
      escalates — no infinite Developer↔QA ping-pong burning tokens overnight.
    

    

      Stuck and abandoned work is detectable.

      Packages can be blocked on a dependency, a decision, or something
      external. A pipeline left open too long is flagged as stale and can be resumed or cancelled.
    

    

      The escape hatches leave a trail.

      The Project Manager can reset a rework counter or reopen a cancelled
      package — but every override is recorded with its reason. Recovery never means quietly
      rewriting history.
    

  

  

    This is the slide I would want to see if I were sitting where you are, because "nine agents in a
    chain" invites one obvious question: what happens when one of them gets it wrong?

    The first thing to internalise is that a stage failing is the system working. QA is there to
    fail things. When it does, the ledger routes the package back to the Developer with QA's own
    written failure summary attached, and the Developer picks up exactly what broke. That is a loop
    by design. Earlier you saw red rework badges in the work-package screenshot — that was this
    happening, and the project still completed.

    The second is that the loop is bounded. Every round trip increments a counter on the package,
    and past a threshold the package stops and escalates instead of continuing. That matters most in
    the headless runner, where nobody is watching. Without a circuit breaker, a Developer and a QA
    agent that disagree will happily disagree until you run out of budget. I would rather be told
    the pipeline is stuck.

    Third, work can be legitimately stuck rather than broken — waiting on a dependency, on a
    decision I have not made, on something external. That is a distinct state, not a failure. And a
    pipeline that was started but never finished, because a session crashed or a laptop closed, gets
    flagged as stale so it can be resumed or cancelled deliberately.

    Last, the overrides. The Project Manager can reset a rework counter or reopen a cancelled
    package — the system does not paint you into a corner. But every override is written into the
    ledger with its reason. When I come back in three weeks and wonder why a package with five
    failed rounds shipped, the answer is in the file. Recoverability without an audit trail is just
    a nicer way to lose information.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
Keeping track

  
The integrated web interface has the essentials at a glance and in detail.

  
  

    Plain files are the right storage decision and a poor review surface. Nobody wants to audit a
    project by opening seven JSON files, so the ledger ships a local web GUI that reads the same
    directory.

    What you are looking at is the real project list from my own store, filtered to one product.
    Each row is a project: which repository it belongs to, how many work packages it broke into, how
    far it got, and — the column I would point at — which runner executed it. Some of those ran in
    VS Code with me in the loop. Most ran headless through the orchestrator. Same ledger, same
    personas, and from this view you genuinely cannot tell them apart except by that badge.

    Notice the rework entries in the project names. Those are second and third passes over the same
    feature, filed as their own projects, with their history intact. Nothing is overwritten.

    The tabs across the top are, more or less, the agenda for the rest of this part. Insights is the
    observation channel I mentioned. Knowledge is the store the next slide covers. Strategy is where
    the vision per repository is declared. Orchestrator is live run tracking. Configuration is where
    the model assignments live.

    The reason this matters beyond convenience: oversight is what makes delegating to a nine-stage
    pipeline defensible. I am not asking anyone to trust that it worked. Everything each agent did
    and wrote is inspectable after the fact, and while it is running.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
Knowledge That Persists

  
Elevate curated project insights into institutional memory.

  

    

      
🌍 Global Knowledge

      
Curated cross-repository insights: architectural patterns, tooling decisions, workflow lessons.

Survives across all projects.

    

    

      
📦 Repository Knowledge

      
Codebase-specific facts: conventions, gotchas, module dependencies.

Scoped to one repo, always available.

    

  

  

  

    Synthesis extracts insights → future Planners & PMs query the store before decisions.

    Alongside it sits a strategic vision — which is the next slide.
  

  

    The Knowledge Archiver (subagent of Synthesis) extracts insights at project end. Future projects
    start smarter. Two scopes: global knowledge applies everywhere, repository knowledge is codebase-specific.

    Knowledge is backward-looking — what previous projects learned. The strategic vision on the next
    slide is the forward-looking half of the same idea, and the Planner reads both before it drafts
    anything.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
The architect's vision

  

    Every decision you make is coloured by your vision of where the codebase is going.

    Write it down, and the agents get the same lens.
  

  

    

      Short term
      — what is being worked towards now.
    

    

      Mid term
      — what is coming, and worth leaving room for.
    

    

      Long term
      — the direction that rules approaches out.
    

  

  

    The planner weaves it into the plan — as a result,
    the whole pipeline inherits the vision.
  

  

    Same feature request. Shared vision. A different architecture.
  

  

    This is the most underestimated slide in the deck, so I want to be direct about why it matters.

    As a software architect, this vision lives in me. I don't consult it — I apply it in every decision,
    continuously, whether I'm reviewing a pull request or naming a class. It's not a document I open.
    It's the lens I look through. And that's exactly the problem: an agent doesn't have it. It sees the
    feature request and nothing else.

    Think about what I actually do when handed a feature request. I don't just solve it. I ask what else
    is coming. Is this the third variant of something that should have been generalised two variants
    ago? Is the module I'm about to extend the one being replaced next quarter? Should this be a quick
    fix because the whole area is due for a rewrite, or built properly because it's load-bearing for the
    next two years?

    None of that is answerable from the feature request. It's answerable from the strategy. And it
    doesn't change whether you build the feature — it changes its shape. Same requirement, three
    horizons, three genuinely different architectures.

    Writing the strategy down per repository is what puts that lens in front of the Planner. And here's
    the part that gets overlooked: it doesn't stop at the Planner. It colours the entire plan — the work
    package boundaries, the sequencing, what gets abstracted and what stays concrete. Every stage after
    that works from that plan. The Developer implements against it, the Reviewer evaluates against it,
    the Documentation agent describes it. So the whole pipeline inherits the vision from one declaration,
    without a single downstream persona needing to know it exists.

    Concretely: the Planner calls the ledger for the repository context before it drafts anything. That
    returns the three horizons plus the history of prior projects in this repository. If a vision is
    declared, the Planner validates the plan against it. If none is declared it proceeds anyway — but
    then it's planning purely for today, and you get today's solution.

    One clarification, because the previous slide's footnote could mislead: the vision is declared per
    repository, not per project. It's long-lived context that every project in that repository inherits —
    the right granularity, because strategy outlives features.

    The honest caveat: the strategy is only as good as what you wrote in it. This is not the system
    inferring your roadmap. It's the system making sure your roadmap is in the room when the plan gets
    written, instead of living in your head or in a slide deck nobody opened.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
The Observation Channel

  
Ledger personas make observations on task or task-adjacent matters.

  

    

      Things you would notice
      — a fragile pattern, a missing test, technical debt, possible improvements and refactorings.
    

    

      Captured as it happens
      — appended the moment it's noticed without acting on it, so it does not disrupt the model's workflow.
    

    

      All stages contribute
      — each of the personas record their observations: Developer, QA, Security Auditor, Reviewer and more.
    

  

  

    The ledger records it all.

    This allows consistently leaving the code in a better state than you found it.

  

  

    I called this the observation channel twice already without showing it, so here it is.

    Every agent in the pipeline has one job description and a much wider field of view. The Developer
    is implementing a work package, but while doing that it notices a fragile helper three files over,
    or a naming inconsistency that has nothing to do with today's task. QA is verifying acceptance
    criteria, but it also notices a test gap nobody asked it to close. None of that belongs in the
    current work package — fixing it would blur the boundary between what was scoped and what wasn't
    — but none of it should be lost either.

    So it gets written down instead, appended to the project's own log the moment it's noticed. Not
    batched at the end of the session, not reconstructed from memory during the wrap-up — captured at
    the actual moment of contact with the code, because that is the only moment the observation is
    cheap and complete. Wait until later and you get a plausible-sounding summary instead of what was
    actually seen.

    Each specialist writes in its own vocabulary — a code smell, a piece of technical debt, an
    accessibility gap, a security concern — but the shape is the same everywhere: what was noticed,
    where, and how urgent it is.

    None of this is the verdict. It's raw material. What happens to it next is the knowledge slide you
    already saw: Synthesis reads the accumulated log at the end of the project and distills it into
    the knowledge store, so the next project — potentially in a different repository — starts a
    little smarter than this one did.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

  
Choosing the Model per Persona

  
Not every persona needs the strongest model. Each one declares its own.

  

    

      Reasoning-heavy personas get the stronger model.

      Planner and Project Manager — the roles where a bad decision
      propagates through everything downstream.
    

    

      Execution personas run on the default.

      Developer, QA, Reviewer, Documentation — well-scoped work
      against a plan that has already been thought through.
    

    

      Assignments live outside the persona text.

      A model registry maps personas to models, editable in the GUI.
      Swapping a model does not mean touching a single persona document.
    

  

  

    A practical question that comes up as soon as anyone considers running this seriously: which model
    runs which persona?

    Worth being precise here: the model is bound to the persona, not to a slot in the workflow. In the
    ledger workflow the two happen to line up one-to-one, but the same persona used standalone outside
    the workflow carries the same model assignment with it.

    The principle is that the value of a stronger model is highest where judgement compounds. If the
    Planner scopes the work badly, or the Project Manager sequences the packages wrongly, everything
    after it inherits the mistake. Those two are worth the stronger model. The Developer working
    against a good plan, the QA agent running the tests, the Documentation agent updating a manifest —
    that's well-bounded work, and the default model handles it.

    The important design point is where the assignment lives. It is not written into the persona
    documents. There's a separate registry that maps each persona to a model, with a default for
    everything unassigned, and it's editable through the GUI. When a new model version lands you
    change the registry and rebuild — you don't go editing 24 persona files.

    I'm deliberately not putting cost figures on this slide, because I haven't measured them properly.
    The reasoning here is about where judgement matters, not about a spend calculation. If anyone wants
    to talk cost, I'd rather do it in questions and be honest about what I don't know.
  






  
Interconnecting multiple agents

For developers: Same workflow, headless in the command line.

Part 4

  
Working With Models

  
Understanding limits & bringing structure.






  
Working With Models

  
Every Session Starts From Zero

  

    Every session, the model discovers your project anew.

    Make that easy & fast.
  

  

    
› Technical manifest
      — pre-fetched codebase knowledge: beats the codebase search.

    
› Domain briefs
      — what the business actually does, in its own vocabulary.

    
› Institutional knowledge
      — the things everyone knows and nobody wrote down.

    
› System architecture
      — the wider landscape, and a “you are here” marker on it.

    
› Project vision
      — short, mid and long term.

    
› Glossary
      — ties all of the above together.

  

  

    This is the foundation for any meaningful agentic work.
  

  

    The best persona in the world cannot compensate for project knowledge nobody has written down.
  

  

    If there is one piece of homework to take from this talk, it's this slide — and it's the one that
    pays off regardless of which tools you end up using.

    Start with the amnesia. The agent that picks up your task has never seen your project. Not "has
    forgotten" — has never seen it. That happens again on the next request, and the one after. You can
    either let it rediscover the project every time, or you can write the project down once and hand it
    over.

    On the manifest specifically: pre-fetched knowledge beats search, and that surprises people. Letting
    an agent grep its way around a codebase works, but it's slow, it burns context on dead ends, and
    what it finds depends on what it happened to search for. A manifest that states the architecture,
    the public interfaces, the conventions and the file tree up front is both cheaper and more reliable.
    In this repo that's the project manifest — and there's a rule that if the code contradicts the
    manifest, the code is probably what's wrong.

    Being straight about what's in place here: the technical manifest, the file tree, the architecture
    documents and the vision are all real and in daily use. Domain briefs and a proper glossary are on
    the list rather than done. I'm putting them on the slide because the need for them is what I keep
    running into, not because I've solved them.

    The two that non-developers will care about most are institutional knowledge and the glossary. That's
    exactly what the business-engineer workspace from Part 1 is — a division's knowledge written down
    somewhere an agent can read it. And the glossary matters more than it sounds: most of the confusion
    I've seen between an agent and a project comes down to one word meaning two different things.

    Last point, and it connects back to AX: none of this is documentation you write for the agent's
    benefit alone. A new colleague needs all six of these too. The agent just makes the absence
    impossible to ignore, because it never quietly works around the gap.
  






  
Working With Models

  
Treat Models Like a Colleague

  

    Not a tool. Not an oracle. A capable colleague that works for you.
  

  

    
› Fast, and knows the language better than you do.

    
› Has no idea about your last meeting's decisions.

    
› Has the utmost confidence in their abilities.

    
› Will not tell you when they're unsure.

  

  

    Models sound just as sure when they're wrong.
  

  

    This is the mental model I'd most like people to leave with, and it took me a while to arrive at it.

    "Tool" is wrong because a tool doesn't make judgement calls — a hammer doesn't decide where the nail
    goes. "Oracle" is wrong in the other direction, and it's the more expensive mistake, because it
    stops you reviewing.

    Colleague is the closest fit. And once you hold that frame, the right behaviours follow without
    anyone having to prescribe them. You read what a colleague hands you. You ask why they chose that
    approach. You give them the context they'd need to do the job — which is exactly what a persona and
    a well-documented project are.

    The three properties matter in that order. The speed and the language fluency are genuine and
    they're why we're all here. The missing context is manageable, and it's what the rest of this talk
    has been about closing.

    The third one has no equivalent in a human colleague, and that's why it catches people. A colleague
    who is out of their depth signals it — they hesitate, they hedge, they ask a question. The model
    produces a confident answer at the edge of its knowledge in exactly the same tone as a confident
    answer at the centre of it. There is no tell. You cannot calibrate your trust by reading the
    output's confidence, because the confidence is constant.

    Which means the review is not optional, and it doesn't get to be selective either.
  






  
Working With Models

  
Request Crafting

  

    With documentation in place, craft requests with confidence.
  

  

    
› Be verbose, be precise
      — include everything you can think of.

    
› Share your approach
      — already know how part X should be done? Write it down.

    
› Name the pitfalls
      — include that gotcha from last year.

    
› Include your expectations
      — real-world usage scenarios go a long way.

    
› Structure, structure
      — organize it all with headers - useful for you and the model.

    
› Review, then audit
      — read it yourself, use the plan reviewer personas.

  

  

    It's not a race to the shortest prompt: It's about providing sufficient guidance.
  

  

    The hidden foundation of a request is the project's documentation. Weigh what goes into the spec or the docs.
  

  

    The previous slide was the honest limitation. This one is what you actually do about it, and all
    four points are habits rather than tools — they cost nothing to adopt tomorrow morning.

    Start with the limitation restated in one line, because it sets up all four: the model will solve
    the problem you described, correctly and thoroughly, and possibly in entirely the wrong way, because
    it is missing the part you know and did not mention. It will not stop and ask. It builds what was
    asked.

    Be verbose, be precise. This is the one that feels wrong to developers, because we're trained to be
    terse. A one-line request gets a plausible answer to a question you did not quite ask. Say what the
    thing is for, what must not change, which files are in scope, what "done" looks like. The rule of
    thumb I use: whatever constraint I decide is too obvious to state is the one that comes back
    violated.

    Share your own approach. This one surprises people, because there's a worry that you'll bias the
    model into agreeing with you. In practice the opposite is the risk: with no proposal on the table it
    invents one and commits to it. Give it yours and you get a comparison instead of a guess — and
    explicitly invite it to disagree, with reasons. Some of the best design conversations I've had this
    year started with me proposing something mediocre and being talked out of it.

    Name the pitfalls. You know where this codebase bites. The migration that has to run first, the
    class everyone thinks is dead and isn't, the test that passes for the wrong reason. None of that is
    in the code where it can be read. Two lines of warning in the request is the highest-value writing
    you'll do all day. And when you hit a trap that wasn't on your list, that's exactly what the
    knowledge store from Part 3 is for — write it down once so the next session starts with it.

    Review, then audit. Two separate things. Review is you reading what came back, which we covered on
    the last slide and which doesn't get to be selective. Audit is structural: a second agent whose only
    job is to check the first one's work — the Plan Auditor and the Reviewer in the workflow you saw
    earlier. A model is a poor judge of its own output and a fairly good judge of someone else's. That
    asymmetry is worth building on.

    The closing line matters. None of these four steps move the judgement off your desk. What they do is
    make the judgement legible — turn what you know into something the model can act on, instead of
    something it silently works around.
  






  
Working With Models

  
Newer Is Not Simply Better

  

    A new model version is a new colleague, not a promotion for the old one.
  

  

    

      Capability and behaviour can shift.

      Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 for example adhere to instructions far more
      strictly.

      Example: the Plan Auditor 
      .
    

    

      Monitor the first runs with new model versions.

      Changes will become visible in your real world projects. Get a feeling for your interactions, read the model's internal dialogue and verify results.
    

    

      Persona evolution in action.

      Adjusting your personas is expected and encouraged. They are living documents, and fully yours to maintain.
    

  

  

    Within the same version, models also evolve as providers work on them continuously.
  

  
  

    This one costs people real time, so it's worth stating plainly: a version number going up does not
    mean every behaviour got better. It means you have a different colleague now.

    The example is ours and it's recent. The Plan Auditor is deliberately scoped to audit and not to
    rewrite — that separation is what keeps the audit trustworthy. Older models read that as a strong
    preference and would still make a correction if you asked them to. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 read the
    same sentence as a hard constraint and refused, including on direct instruction to fix a defect
    they had just reported.

    Note what happened there. Nothing regressed. The model got better at doing exactly what the
    persona said. Our wording was just looser than we thought it was, and the older model's leniency
    had been quietly covering for it.

    So the practical advice is: when you move to a new model, watch the first few real runs. Benchmarks
    won't tell you this — it only shows up against your personas and your project. And when you find
    something, adjust the persona. That's not a failure of the design, that's the design working. The
    persona is a living document; it's versioned and built from one source precisely so that this kind
    of change is a single edit rather than a hunt through copies.

    If anyone asks whether that means pinning model versions: you can, and for a production pipeline
    it's reasonable. But you'll want to move eventually, and the same audit is waiting for you then.
  






  
Working With Models

  
An IDE Is Not Only for Developers

  

    A workspace you can browse, read, and talk to — that is useful to anyone
    who owns a body of knowledge.
  

  

    

      A business engineer in our division set up an agent workspace to
      hold and maintain the institutional knowledge of the division.
      


      
        › Relevant repositories cloned into the workspace, so the agents can read the real systems.

        › Connected to Jira and Confluence through MCP servers.

        › Specialised personas for discussing projects and the system landscape.
      
      


      The result is a place where you can ask about a project and get an answer grounded in the
      division's own material — and where new colleagues can learn the landscape.
    

  

  

    Not a single line of code written. Structure, documents, and personas.
  

  

    This is the slide for everyone in the room who is not a developer — and it's a real example, not a
    hypothetical.

    What an IDE actually gives you is three things: a file tree you can navigate, files you can read,
    and a chat that can see both. None of that is inherently technical. It happens to be where
    developers live, so that's where the good tooling landed first.

    What makes this example work is that the agents can read the actual source material — the
    repositories are in the workspace, and Jira and Confluence are connected through MCP servers,
    which I'll come back to in Part 3. The agents aren't recalling things from training data. They're
    reading the division's own documents.

    The takeaway for the team leads and section heads: the barrier here is not programming ability.
    It's being willing to organise your material and describe the specialists you want. If you own a
    domain, you can build this.
  






  
Working With Models

  
Personas and Skills

  
Clear boundaries make skills effective.

  

    

      
Persona

      

        The profession.

        

        A developer, copywriter, designer, etc. Has identity, values, standards,
        and a workflow.

        

        "I know what my job is and how to do it well."

        

        › Loaded for a whole session.
      

    

    

      
Skill

      

        A specific task, workflow or capability.

        

        Often project-specific: A software release check, updating the changelog with 
        a particular writing style, etc.

        

        "How to do X in project Y."

        

        › Invoked on demand.
      

    

  

  

    💡 Tip: Keep skills slim. The knowledge they need belongs in the project manifest, 
    and the skills point there.
  

  

    This is the question I get asked most often, so it's worth being crisp about it.

    The persona is the colleague. The skill is the runbook on their desk. You don't rewrite someone's
    job description because a deployment procedure changed — you update the runbook.

    Concrete example from this repo: the Developer persona knows how to implement a plan, review its
    own work, and capture insights. That's the persona. But "check whether this project is ready to
    tag a release" is project-specific — seven checks, in a fixed order, particular to this codebase.
    That's the release-check skill, and it lives with the project rather than with the persona.

    On slimness: the skills in this repo are deliberately short. When a skill needs a lot of
    background, that background goes into a reference document and the skill links to it. Both models
    and humans skim long documents, and a skipped step in a procedure is worse than no procedure.

    Skills are built and deployed by the same pipeline as personas — source files in, platform-specific
    output for VS Code and Claude Code out. Same discipline, different artifact.
  






  
Working With Models

  
AX — Agent Experience

  

    Developer Experience, but for the agent working in your project.
  

  

    

      The agents report their own friction.

      Missing tooling, a script that only half exists, documentation that
      contradicts the code, a handoff that arrived without the data it promised.
    

    

      It goes into the ledger, not into the void.

      Observations accumulate across work packages and land in the
      synthesis report at the end of the project.
    

    

      Then you fix the environment.

      Add the missing script, correct the stale document, tighten the
      handoff. The next run is smoother — for the agents and for you.
    

  

  

    Friction that slows an agent down is usually slowing your colleagues down too.
  

  

    AX is a term I've started using deliberately, by analogy with DX. If Developer Experience is about
    how pleasant a codebase is to work in, Agent Experience is the same question asked about the agent.

    The mechanism is simple: every persona ends its session by reporting genuine friction it hit —
    tooling that was missing, a script that didn't do what its documentation claimed, context it needed
    and couldn't find. Most sessions report nothing, and that's the expected outcome. The value is in
    the exceptions.

    Two things make this worth having. First, an agent has no social reason to stay quiet. It won't
    decide the missing script is too small to mention, and it won't assume it's the only one who
    couldn't find the document. Second, it hits your project cold, every single time. It has no
    accumulated workarounds, so it trips over exactly the things a new team member would trip over.

    The pattern I keep seeing: the friction the agents report is almost never agent-specific. Stale
    documentation, an undocumented build step, a script that needs three environment variables nobody
    wrote down — that's the onboarding experience for humans as well. Fixing it for the agent fixes it
    for everyone.
  






  
Key Takeaways

  

  

    

      1. Personas bring engineering rigor to AI instructions.

      Not prompts — operating manuals. Versioned, templated, validated.
    

    

      2. Agent personas are useful for everyone.

      Engineer your own personas - for both business and private use.
    

    

      3. A shared ledger turns isolated sessions into a coordinated team.

      Persistent memory + automatic handoffs + collective intelligence.
    

    

      4. This approach works today, with tools you already have.

      VS Code, Claude Code, Gemini, ChatGPT — personas work across all of them.
    

    

      5. Structure closes the context gap. You still close the judgement gap.

      A capable colleague who was never in the room — and never says they're unsure.
    

  

  

    Five things to remember. Personas are engineering artifacts. They're for everyone, not just
    developers. The ledger creates a team. You can start today with what you already have.

    And the fifth one is the one I'd most want to survive the walk back to the desk: all of this reduces
    what the model doesn't know, and none of it replaces your judgement about whether the work is the
    right work.
  






  
Questions

  

  
What would you want to try this on?

  

  

    The repository, the Persona Design Guide, and the quickstart guide are linked on the next slide.
  

  

    Buffer and question slide. The prompt at the top is there on purpose — "any questions?" tends to get
    silence, while a concrete question about their own work usually gets someone started.

    Questions I should be ready for:

    — What does this cost to run? Be honest: I have not measured it properly. What I can say is which
      stages get the stronger model and why.
    — How long does a full workflow run take? Varies with the plan; the honest answer is that the
      bottleneck is usually the human review stages, not the agents.
    — Does it work with our internal models? The model registry is the place that answers this — the
      assignment layer is separate from the personas.
    — How do you stop it going off the rails? Three answers: the plan is reviewed before any code is
      written, the pipeline includes QA, security and review stages, and every stage can send work back.
    — Can I use the personas without the ledger? Yes — that's what the standalone suite is for, and it's
      the right entry point for anyone starting.
    — Is this open? Yes, and the Persona Design Guide is already being used by unrelated projects in
      completely different domains.
